questions.q: How does Solomon describe his lover’s feet in her sandals and the curves of her thighs?
questions.a: He describes her feet in her sandals as beautiful and the curves of her thighs like the work of a craftsman.

questions.q: How does Solomon describe his love’s navel and belly?
questions.a: Solomon describes his love’s navel as a round bowl which never lacks spiced wine and her belly as a mound of wheat surrounded with lilies.

questions.q: How does Solomon describe his lover’s two breasts?
questions.a: Solomon describes her two breasts like two fawns, twins of a gazelle.

questions.q: How does Solomon describe his lover’s neck, eyes, and nose?
questions.a: Solomon describes her neck as an ivory tower, her eyes like a pool, and her nose like the tower of Lebanon.

questions.q: How does Solomon describe his lover’s head and hair?
questions.a: Solomon describes her head like Mount Carmel and her hair like purple, captivating him.

questions.q: How does Solomon describe his lover and her breasts?
questions.a: He describes her height as a date palm tree and her breasts as date clusters.

questions.q: What does he also want his lover’s breasts and breath to be like?
questions.a: He also wants his lover’s breasts to be like date clusters and her breath to be sweet like dates and the smell of an apple.

questions.q: What does he want his lover’s mouth to be like?
questions.a: He wants her mouth to be like the best wine.

questions.q: To whom does the young woman belong and whom does he desire?
questions.a: The young woman belongs to her beloved, and her beloved desires her.

questions.q: Where does the young woman want her beloved to go with her?
questions.a: She wants him to go into the countryside to spend the night in the villages.

questions.q: Why does she want her beloved to rise early?
questions.a: She wants him to rise early to see if the vines in the vineyards have budded and if the pomegranates have begun blooming.

questions.q: What does she say she will give to her beloved when they get to the vineyards?
questions.a: She says she will give him her love.

questions.q: What does she say the mandrakes would do?
questions.a: She says the mandrakes would give off their fragrance.

questions.q: What does she say was at the door where she and her lover were staying?
questions.a: She says that at the door where they were staying there were all sorts of choice fruits, new and old, that she had stored up for him.

commentary.text: The graces of the church. (Song 7:1-9) The delight of the church in Christ. (Song 7:10-13)

Song 7:1-9 The similitudes here are different from what they were before, and in the original refer to glorious and splendid clothing. Such honour have all his saints; and having put on Christ, they are distinguished by their beautiful and glorious apparel. They adorn the doctrine of God their Saviour in all things. Consistent believers honour Christ, recommend the gospel, and convince and awaken sinners. The church resembles the stately and spreading palm; while her love for Christ, and the obedience resulting therefrom, are precious fruit of the true Vine. The King is held in the galleries. Christ takes delight in the assemblies and ordinances of his people; and admires the fruit of his grace in them. When applied to the church and to each faithful Christian, all this denotes that beauty of holiness, in which they shall be presented to their heavenly Bridegroom.

Song 7:10-13 The church, the believing soul, triumphs in its relation to Christ, and interest in him. She humbly desires communion with him. Let us walk together, that I may receive counsel, instruction, and comfort from thee; and may make known my wants and my grievances to thee, with freedom, and without interruption. Communion with Christ is what all that are made holy earnestly breathe after. And those who would converse with Christ, must go forth from the world. Wherever we are, we may keep up communion with God. Nor should we go where we cannot in faith ask him to go with us. Those who would go abroad with Christ, must begin early in the morning of their days; must begin every day with him, seek him early, seek him diligently. A gracious soul can reconcile itself to the poorest places, if it may have communion with God in them; but the most delightful fields will not satisfy, unless the Beloved is there. Let us not think to be satisfied with any earthly object. Our own souls are our vineyards; they should be planted with useful trees. We should often search whether we are fruitful in righteousness. Christ's presence will make the vine flourish, and the tender grapes appear, as the returning sun revives the gardens. If we can appeal to him, Thou knowest all things, thou knowest that I love thee; if his Spirit witness with our spirit, that our souls prosper, it is enough. And we must beg of him to search and try us, to discover us to ourselves. The fruits and exercises of graces are pleasant to the Lord Jesus. These must be laid up, and always ready; that by our bringing forth much fruit, he may be glorified. It is all from him, therefore it is fit it should be all for him.
